Raising for an AI company

Analysislowob research

By lowob · 22 April 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

In short: Investors now price AI application companies on workflow ownership, margin and retention, so raise on that evidence and put the model in the appendix. The money is there: AI companies took 82.7% of US venture deal value through September 2026. But a large share went to a handful of model companies, and the application companies that raise well show what any software company shows, plus two numbers only AI companies carry: gross margin after inference, and what happens when the model provider ships their feature.

This is operating guidance, not investment advice.

Key points

  • AI took 82.7% of US venture deal value through Q3 2026, and 60.7% of capital raised on Carta's platform in Q1 2026.
  • OpenAI and Anthropic alone took 43% of global startup funding in the first half of 2026, so the headline AI total says little about application rounds.
  • Application companies are priced on retention, margin, distribution and replaceability, with inference cost and platform risk on top.
  • Enterprise buyers moved fast between model providers in 2026, so a tested ability to switch models is evidence, not a claim.
  • Credits are runway, not revenue: show them as a cost reduction with an expiry date.

The market has split

Two years ago "AI" in the deck earned a premium on its own. That has ended for application companies. Investors now sort the market into model companies and the companies that build on them. The two get priced on different logic.

The funding data shows the split. Crunchbase found OpenAI and Anthropic together raised $217 billion, or 43% of all global startup funding, in the first half of 2026. The PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor put AI at 82.7% of US deal value through September. Carta's first-quarter data is more useful for most founders: 60.7% of capital raised on its platform went to AI companies, 14.2% to foundation model companies, and 83% of capital raised by SaaS companies went to those building with AI. In software, almost everyone is now an AI company, which means the label no longer differentiates.

Model companies are priced on capability, compute access and research talent. Most founders reading this are not building one. Application companies are priced on what any software company is priced on: retention, margin, distribution and how hard the product is to replace.

The difference is that an AI application carries two extra costs. Inference, which hits gross margin. And platform risk, because the model provider can ship your feature. The model is not the product covered how to answer the "wrapper" objection. This piece is about how that answer shows up in a raise.

The five questions you will get

Expect these in the first meeting, not the last.

  1. Gross margin after inference. Investors want the number net of model and compute costs, and they want the trend. A flat or rising cost per task is a problem. A falling one is a story. Our explainer on AI inference cost sets out what drives the number.
  2. What happens when the provider ships your feature. The honest answer is that some of your product will be absorbed. The question is what remains. Data, distribution or workflow depth are the three defensible answers.
  3. Model dependency and switching cost. Can you move to another model in a week, a month, or never? Have you done it? A company that has swapped models once is more fundable than one that says it could.
  4. Data rights. Do your contracts let you use customer data to improve the product? Many early contracts do not, because nobody asked. Fix that before the raise, not during it. A clear data processing agreement is where the answer lives.
  5. Paid or free usage. Free-tier activity is not evidence of demand. It is acquisition cost. Investors will strip it out, so strip it out first.

The switching question has become sharper in 2026. Menlo Ventures' enterprise survey, published in November 2026, found Anthropic's share of enterprise API spend rose from 40% to 55% in a year, OpenAI's from 27% to 31%, and Google's fell from 21% to 9%. Shares that move that fast mean a company locked to one provider is exposed to that provider's pricing, quality and roadmap. Menlo also found buyers prioritise capability over cost when choosing models, so the cheapest model is rarely the end state.

The evidence that counts

Raise against evidence, not narrative argued for raising on what customers have done rather than on the story. For an AI company the evidence has four parts.

EvidenceWhat it provesHow to show it
Production usage with retentionThe product does a job every weekTeams active weekly and still there at 90 days, paid only
Gross margin trendThe business survives its inference billThree or more months net of inference, moving the right way
Falling cost per taskThe margin story is operational, not hoped forCaching, routing to cheaper models, prompt reduction, with dates
Security pack that passed reviewEnterprise buyers can actually signA real buyer's security process, completed

Cost per task is where the work shows. Prompt caching and routing simpler requests to smaller models are the usual first moves. Record what each change did to the number.

A security pack that has been through a real buyer's process is worth more than any claim about enterprise readiness. The pilot that survives security review covered the pack, and our explainer on SOC 2 for AI vendors covers what an attestation does and does not prove.

A company that has swapped models once is more fundable than one that says it could.

The capital stack

An AI raise usually has more than one source of capital, and they do not behave the same way.

SourceWhat it is forWhat it is not
EquityRunway, hiring, go-to-marketCheap, or quick
Cloud and model creditsReducing inference cost for a periodRevenue, or margin
Startup programmesCredits, introductions, sometimes distributionValidation of the business
Strategic investorsDistribution or data accessNeutral capital

Credits are runway, not revenue. Show them in the plan as a cost reduction with an end date. Do not let them flatter the margin line in the pitch. Investors will find the expiry date and ask what margin looks like after it.

Strategic investors from cloud or model providers want something: distribution of their platform, or data from your use case. That can be a good trade. Know what you are giving before you take the cheque, and keep model switching possible in the terms. Corporate investors are now everywhere in large rounds: PitchBook data reported in August 2026 found corporate venture arms involved in 82.6% of US deal value in 2026.

Narrative discipline

The deck should read like a software company that happens to use AI, not an AI company looking for a use case.

Lead with the customer and the workflow. Which job, for which team, replacing what. Then the evidence from the section above. Then the market and the plan. Menlo's survey found new budgets funded 55% of incremental enterprise AI spend in 2026, against 22% from existing software budgets. If your buyer is funding you from a new budget line, say whose line it is and who signs it.

The model, the architecture and the eval results go in the appendix. They matter in diligence. They do not carry the first meeting, and leading with them signals that you have not found the customer yet.

Run the round the way Run the round like a sales process describes: a pipeline, a timeline, a named owner. PitchBook's second-quarter report noted that time between rounds has compressed, especially for AI companies. AI investors are busy and have seen a lot of similar decks. A tight process is itself evidence.

lowob takeaways

  • The AI label no longer differentiates. Investors price applications like software companies, plus inference and platform risk.
  • Show margin net of inference, with a trend. Falling cost per task is the operating proof.
  • Test model switching before the raise. Provider shares moved by double digits in a year.
  • Credits are a cost reduction with an expiry date. Never let them flatter the margin line.

Common questions

How do investors value AI application startups?

On what any software company is priced on: retention, margin, distribution and how hard the product is to replace. AI applications also carry inference cost and platform risk, so investors ask for gross margin net of inference and evidence of model switching.

What questions will investors ask an AI startup?

Gross margin after inference, what happens when the model provider ships your feature, model dependency and switching cost, data rights in customer contracts, and how much usage is paid versus free.

Should cloud credits count as revenue in an AI startup pitch?

No. Credits are runway, not revenue. Show them as a cost reduction with an end date, because investors will find the expiry date and ask what margin looks like after it.

How much venture funding goes to AI startups in 2026?

AI companies took 82.7% of US venture deal value through September 2026, per PitchBook-NVCA. Much of it went to a few model companies: OpenAI and Anthropic took 43% of global startup funding in the first half, per Crunchbase.

Sources and notes

  • PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, Q3 2026, October 2026. US data through September 2026, taken from the NVCA summary page.
  • Carta, State of Private Markets Q1 2026, 29 May 2026. Companies on Carta's platform; AI classification is Carta's.
  • Crunchbase News, Global startup investment hit record $510B in H1 2026, 2 July 2026. Global data; dominated by frontier lab rounds.
  • Menlo Ventures, 2026: The State of Enterprise AI, 3 November 2026. Investor research; survey of nearly 400 US enterprise decision makers fielded by Morning Consult, 8 to 26 September 2026. Menlo is an investor in AI companies.
  • PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, Q2 2026, data as of 30 June 2026. US only; the time-between-rounds point is qualitative in the report.
  • The Next Web, Megadeals took 87.5% of US venture dollars, 12 August 2026. News report on PitchBook data; corporate venture participation figure.
  • The five questions, evidence table and capital stack are lowob's framework.

Next Move

Calculate gross margin net of inference for each of the last three months, and cost per task for your highest-volume workflow. If you have never run that workflow on a second model, run it this week and record the time, cost and quality difference.
